doc.title: John Budd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [transcript only]

title: Medicine, baseball and music turning into businesses; what professionalism means
summary: Budd says all three fields became business rather than profession, and discusses selfless professionalism among musicians.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: It’d be fine. Yes, because I feel that very strongly. The older I get the more I realize that the baseball has sort of left me behind because there have become millionaires and tremendous ability, but it’s become a business, no longer just a baseball game. And of course the same thing has happened in music. What’s happening in music is shocking to me at my age, and my tastes in music, and the same thing has happened in medicine. Medicine, which used to be a profession, now is like a business and it’s seen by the © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -1-
competition in doctors, insurance companies, hospitals, patients, and lawyers, to get the best they can and provide the best they can, and it’s different.
Well the idea of a profession, are you saying that people don’t do it because they’re as passionate about it as they used to be?

Well that may be I don’t know. But there’s something to that, that the passion is — the passionate move is money, prestige and so forth. And the three professions I guess they used to tell us were medicine, law and the liturgy. Now professions are anything in the world. Professionalism means great ability. But it’s not only that, but professionalism is having a selfless attitude toward helping somebody else I think. Maybe that’s a mistake I have, and I’m not putting it down at all. But I’m glad to be considered one although when I talk to these musicians, if they are professional I am a ham.

No I think you’re right because one thing that people talk about, when you hear musicians talk about other musicians, and what a professional he is, they almost always mention that when they are playing the music, they are most concerned about how the whole thing sounds.
So that is their version of professionalism.

Well it’s a good one. It is indeed. And they are. And they do care for each other and they listen to each other and they don’t ever say out and out “he doesn’t play as well as I do.” They sometimes say “I wish I could do something as well as he did,” they envy each other, but they don’t put each other down very often. I don’t think they do.
